title: Autonomic Nervous System Foundations
summary: Sympathetic and parasympathetic anatomy, transmitters and receptors as the map for autonomic drugs.

lessons.title: Anatomy of the Autonomic Nervous System

levels.kid:
Your body has an **autopilot**. It runs things you never think about: your heartbeat, your breathing speed, your tummy digesting food, your sweat.

The autopilot has two sides. The **fight-or-flight** side gets you ready for action. Your heart beats faster and your eyes open wide, like when a dog barks at you.

The **rest-and-digest** side calms you down. Your heart slows and your tummy gets to work on lunch.

Both sides send messages along nerves, and they use special chemical messengers to talk to your organs.
levels.hs:
The **autonomic nervous system (ANS)** controls involuntary functions: heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, pupils, sweating and bladder. It has two main divisions, plus the enteric nervous system in the gut wall.

**Sympathetic (fight or flight).** Nerves leave the spinal cord in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments (T1–L2). They synapse in a chain of ganglia next to the spine or in ganglia in front of the aorta, so the first neuron is short and the second is long. The **adrenal medulla** is a special case: it releases epinephrine straight into the blood.

**Parasympathetic (rest and digest).** Nerves leave the brainstem in cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X, and the sacral spinal cord (S2–S4). Their ganglia sit near or inside the target organs, so the first neuron is long and the second is short. The **vagus nerve** (CN X) supplies the heart, lungs and most of the gut.

**Messengers.** Every first neuron in both systems releases **acetylcholine**. Second parasympathetic neurons also release acetylcholine; second sympathetic neurons mostly release **norepinephrine**. That is why so many drugs act on acetylcholine or norepinephrine receptors.
levels.college:
**Two-neuron pathway.** Unlike somatic motor neurons, which run directly from the CNS to skeletal muscle and release ACh onto **NM nicotinic** receptors, autonomic pathways have a preganglionic neuron (cell body in the CNS) and a postganglionic neuron (cell body in a peripheral ganglion).

**Sympathetic (thoracolumbar).** Preganglionic cell bodies sit in the intermediolateral cell column of T1–L2. Axons exit via ventral roots and white rami to synapse in **paravertebral** chain ganglia (including the superior cervical ganglion for the head) or pass through as splanchnic nerves to **prevertebral** ganglia (celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric). One preganglionic fiber diverges onto many postganglionic neurons, allowing widespread responses. Postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine, with exceptions:
- **Sweat glands**: sympathetic cholinergic, acting on muscarinic receptors.
- **Adrenal medulla**: chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic neurons stimulated directly by preganglionic ACh; they secrete mostly epinephrine into blood.
- **Renal vascular smooth muscle**: dopamine acting on D1 receptors.

**Parasympathetic (craniosacral).**
- CN III → ciliary ganglion → pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle.
- CN VII → pterygopalatine ganglion (lacrimal gland) and submandibular ganglion (submandibular and sublingual glands).
- CN IX → otic ganglion → parotid.
- CN X → thoracic and abdominal viscera to roughly the splenic flexure.
- S2–S4 pelvic splanchnic nerves → distal colon, bladder, pelvic organs.

**Receptors at the ganglia:** all autonomic ganglia use **NN nicotinic** receptors, so ganglionic blockers affect both divisions.

**Central control:** the hypothalamus, nucleus tractus solitarius, rostral ventrolateral medulla and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus integrate autonomic output.
levels.phd:
The textbook dichotomy of opposing systems understates the ANS's organization. Sympathetic outflow is **functionally specific**: separate preganglionic pools target muscle vasculature, skin vasculature, sudomotor fibers and viscera, and they can be recruited differently (cold activates cutaneous vasoconstrictor fibers; exercise and mental stress favor others). Microneurography of muscle sympathetic nerve activity in humans shows bursts locked to the cardiac cycle and gated by baroreceptor input.

**Cotransmission** is the rule. Sympathetic terminals release ATP (fast P2X-mediated vasoconstriction) and neuropeptide Y (slow, sustained vasoconstriction, potentiating NE) alongside norepinephrine; parasympathetic and enteric neurons release VIP and nitric oxide (nitrergic, NANC transmission). This explains residual neurogenic responses after adrenergic or muscarinic blockade.

The **enteric nervous system**, with the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses, contains on the order of hundreds of millions of neurons and can run peristalsis and secretion autonomously; extrinsic inputs modulate rather than command it.

A 2016 developmental study (Espinosa-Medina and colleagues) argued that sacral preganglionic neurons share transcriptional identity with thoracolumbar sympathetic neurons, proposing that pelvic autonomic outflow is sympathetic. The reclassification remains debated, but it highlights that "parasympathetic" is partly a functional, not developmental, label.

**Neurosurgical anatomy.** The oculosympathetic pathway is a three-neuron chain: hypothalamus → ciliospinal center of Budge (C8–T2) → superior cervical ganglion → fibers along the internal carotid artery to the dilator pupillae and superior tarsal muscle. Lesions anywhere produce **Horner syndrome** (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis depending on level). Spinal cord injury above T6 disconnects splanchnic sympathetic outflow from supraspinal control, producing **neurogenic shock** acutely and **autonomic dysreflexia** chronically.
levels.expert:
For clinicians, ANS anatomy is localization. **Horner syndrome** is the classic test: a small pupil with mild ptosis on one side, anisocoria greater in dim light, and sometimes facial anhidrosis.
- First-order lesions (hypothalamus, brainstem, cervical cord): lateral medullary stroke, syrinx, demyelination.
- Second-order (preganglionic): Pancoast tumor at the lung apex, neck or thoracic surgery, cervical rib.
- Third-order (postganglionic): **internal carotid artery dissection** (painful Horner with neck pain or headache, which is an emergency because of stroke risk), cavernous sinus lesions, cluster headache. Facial sweating is usually spared because those fibers follow the external carotid.

Pharmacologic testing exploits denervation supersensitivity and transmitter release. **Apraclonidine** drops cause the Horner pupil to dilate and the ptosis to improve (reversal of anisocoria), because the denervated dilator upregulates α1 receptors; normal pupils barely respond. **Cocaine** drops block norepinephrine reuptake and dilate a normal pupil but not a sympathetically denervated one. **Hydroxyamphetamine** distinguishes postganglionic lesions (no dilation, because the terminal is gone) from pre-ganglionic ones.

**Spinal cord injury.** Above roughly T6, acute injury can cause neurogenic shock: hypotension with bradycardia (unopposed vagal tone), warm peripheries. Treat with fluids and vasopressors that include β1 and α1 activity (norepinephrine), plus atropine or pacing for bradycardia, since phenylephrine alone can worsen bradycardia reflexively. Later, autonomic dysreflexia (a full bladder or bowel triggering massive sympathetic discharge below the lesion) produces severe hypertension, headache and flushing above the lesion; the first step is to sit the patient up and remove the stimulus.

**Skull base and neck surgery** puts cranial parasympathetic fibers at risk: greater superficial petrosal injury causes dry eye; chorda tympani and otic pathways affect salivation.

keyPoints: ANS divisions: sympathetic (thoracolumbar T1–L2), parasympathetic (craniosacral: CN III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4), enteric
All preganglionic neurons release ACh onto NN nicotinic receptors
Postganglionic parasympathetic = ACh (muscarinic); postganglionic sympathetic = mostly NE
Exceptions: sweat glands (sympathetic cholinergic), adrenal medulla (epinephrine into blood), renal vessels (dopamine)
Horner syndrome = interruption of the 3-neuron oculosympathetic pathway: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis
Cord injury above T6: neurogenic shock acutely, autonomic dysreflexia chronically

lessons.title: Cholinergic Transmission

levels.kid:
Nerves talk to each other and to muscles by passing tiny chemical notes. One of the most important notes is called **acetylcholine**.

The nerve makes acetylcholine and keeps it in little bubbles. When a signal arrives, the bubbles pop open and the notes float across a tiny gap. They land on special catchers on the next cell, and that cell gets the message.

Then a cleanup helper called **acetylcholinesterase** chops up the notes super fast, so the message is short and clear. Some medicines work by slowing down the cleanup helper.
levels.hs:
**Acetylcholine (ACh)** is the transmitter of all autonomic ganglia, parasympathetic nerve endings, sympathetic nerves to sweat glands, the neuromuscular junction and many brain pathways.

The life cycle of ACh:
- **Synthesis**: the enzyme choline acetyltransferase joins choline and acetyl-CoA.
- **Choline uptake**: a transporter brings choline into the nerve ending. This is the slowest, rate-limiting step.
- **Storage**: ACh is pumped into vesicles.
- **Release**: an action potential opens calcium channels; calcium triggers vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release ACh. **Botulinum toxin** blocks this step, causing paralysis.
- **Action**: ACh binds **nicotinic** receptors (ion channels, fast) or **muscarinic** receptors (G protein-coupled, slower).
- **Termination**: **acetylcholinesterase** breaks ACh into choline and acetate in a fraction of a millisecond. Choline is recycled.

Nicotinic receptors are found at ganglia and at skeletal muscle. Muscarinic receptors (M1–M5) are on organs supplied by parasympathetic nerves, like the heart, glands and smooth muscle. Drugs can mimic ACh, block its receptors, or block acetylcholinesterase.
levels.college:
**Synthesis.** Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) transfers an acetyl group from mitochondrial-derived acetyl-CoA to choline in the cytoplasm. Choline is taken up by the high-affinity, Na+-dependent **choline transporter (CHT1)**, the rate-limiting step, which is blocked experimentally by **hemicholinium-3**.

**Storage.** The **vesicular ACh transporter (VAChT)** exchanges protons for ACh, driven by the vesicular H+-ATPase; **vesamicol** blocks it. Vesicles also contain ATP and peptides.

**Release.** Depolarization opens N- and P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. Ca2+ binds synaptotagmin and the SNARE complex (synaptobrevin/VAMP, syntaxin, SNAP-25) drives fusion. **Botulinum toxins** are zinc proteases: type A cleaves SNAP-25, type B cleaves synaptobrevin. **Lambert–Eaton syndrome** autoantibodies target P/Q-type channels. **α-latrotoxin** (black widow) triggers massive release.

**Receptors.**
- **Nicotinic**: pentameric ligand-gated cation channels. Muscle (NM): (α1)2β1δε in adults. Ganglionic (NN): mainly α3β4. CNS: α4β2 and α7.
- **Muscarinic**: GPCRs. **M1, M3, M5** couple to Gq (PLC → IP3/DAG → Ca2+). **M2, M4** couple to Gi/o (↓cAMP; βγ subunits open GIRK K+ channels). M2 dominates in the heart; M3 in smooth muscle, glands and endothelium.
- Presynaptic M2/M4 autoreceptors inhibit further ACh release.

**Termination.** **Acetylcholinesterase (AChE)** is anchored in the synaptic cleft (at the NMJ, to the basal lamina via collagen Q) and is one of the fastest enzymes known. **Butyrylcholinesterase** (plasma or pseudocholinesterase), made in the liver, hydrolyzes succinylcholine, mivacurium and ester local anesthetics; genetic variants prolong succinylcholine paralysis.
levels.phd:
AChE operates near the diffusion limit, with a turnover on the order of 10^4 molecules per second. Its active site lies at the bottom of a deep, narrow **gorge** lined with aromatic residues. The catalytic triad (Ser203, His447, Glu334 in human numbering) performs nucleophilic attack via serine, forming an acetyl-enzyme intermediate that is hydrolyzed in microseconds. A **choline-binding (anionic) subsite** uses cation–π interactions with Trp86 to orient the quaternary ammonium, and a **peripheral anionic site** at the gorge rim (Trp286) binds ligands such as donepezil's benzyl moiety and propidium. This architecture explains inhibitor pharmacology: carbamates and organophosphates acylate Ser203 but deacylate slowly, while reversible inhibitors occupy the gorge noncovalently.

Muscarinic receptor pharmacology is constrained by a highly conserved orthosteric site across M1–M5, which is why subtype-selective orthosteric ligands are rare. Crystal structures of M2 and M3 (2012 onward) revealed less conserved **allosteric vestibules** above the orthosteric pocket, motivating positive allosteric modulators for M1 and M4 in cognition and psychosis.

Nicotinic receptors are Cys-loop channels: each subunit has four transmembrane helices, M2 lines the pore, and ACh binds at subunit interfaces (α–δ and α–ε at muscle). Binding of two agonist molecules sharply increases open probability. Prolonged agonist exposure drives **desensitization** to high-affinity closed states; this, plus sustained depolarization inactivating perijunctional Na+ channels, underlies phase I and phase II depolarizing block.

The neuromuscular junction has a **safety factor**: each impulse normally releases far more ACh and activates far more receptors than needed to reach threshold. Myasthenia gravis, Lambert–Eaton syndrome and nondepolarizing blockers all erode this margin, which is why fatigue appears only once a large fraction of receptors is lost or occupied.
levels.expert:
Clinicians manipulate every step of cholinergic transmission:
- **Release**: botulinum toxin A injections for spasticity, cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, chronic migraine and sialorrhea. Effects last months because nerve terminals must sprout new release sites. Iatrogenic botulism and distant spread are rare risks. Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) blocks K+ channels, prolongs the presynaptic action potential and increases Ca2+ entry in Lambert–Eaton syndrome.
- **Receptors**: muscarinic agonists and antagonists; neuromuscular blockers at NM receptors.
- **Breakdown**: cholinesterase inhibitors for myasthenia, dementia and reversal of neuromuscular blockade.

**Butyrylcholinesterase deficiency** is the bedside classic. A patient given succinylcholine for a rapid sequence intubation who stays paralyzed for hours may carry an atypical BChE variant (dibucaine number testing characterizes it). Management is continued sedation and ventilation until recovery; the anesthesia record should flag it for the patient and relatives. Acquired low BChE (liver disease, pregnancy, organophosphate exposure) prolongs block less dramatically.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Intramuscular botulinum toxin and intrathecal baclofen pumps are both spasticity tools; recognizing iatrogenic weakness or dysphagia after toxin injections matters. In the ICU, anticholinergic burden from many drugs (antihistamines, tricyclics, oxybutynin, some antipsychotics) is a reversible contributor to delirium.

**Mental model:** the cholinergic synapse is fast because termination is enzymatic and local. Any drug that slows termination amplifies whatever ACh is already being released. That is why cholinesterase inhibitors help where some transmission remains (myasthenia, partial blockade) but cannot rescue a junction with no ACh release or no receptors, and why they worsen block once the synapse is already flooded.

keyPoints: ACh is made by ChAT from choline + acetyl-CoA; choline uptake (CHT1) is rate-limiting
VAChT loads vesicles; Ca2+-triggered SNARE fusion releases ACh; botulinum toxin cleaves SNAREs
Nicotinic = ligand-gated channels (NM muscle, NN ganglia); muscarinic M1/M3/M5 Gq, M2/M4 Gi
AChE terminates ACh in the cleft; butyrylcholinesterase hydrolyzes succinylcholine and ester local anesthetics
Lambert–Eaton = antibodies to presynaptic P/Q Ca2+ channels

Depleting choline so no ACh can be made
Cleaving SNARE proteins needed for ACh release

test.explain: Odd-numbered muscarinic receptors couple to Gq; M2 and M4 couple to Gi/o.

test.q: The adult muscle nicotinic receptor subunit composition is:
test.explain: Adult NM receptors are (α1)2β1δε; fetal receptors have γ in place of ε.

test.q: Lambert–Eaton syndrome antibodies target:
test.explain: Reduced Ca2+ entry decreases ACh release; it is often associated with small cell lung cancer.

test.q: Which enzyme hydrolyzes succinylcholine?
test.explain: Plasma butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) metabolizes succinylcholine.

test.q: Vesamicol blocks:
test.explain: Vesamicol inhibits the vesicular ACh transporter.

choices: The collagen Q tail anchoring the enzyme
The oxyanion hole at the gorge base
A transmembrane domain in the cell membrane

advancedTest.q: A patient remains paralyzed for hours after succinylcholine. The test that characterizes the likely cause is:
advancedTest.explain: Atypical butyrylcholinesterase is inhibited less by dibucaine; the dibucaine number identifies the variant.

choices: No ACh is being released to amplify
advancedTest.explain: Cholinesterase inhibitors only prolong ACh that is released; botulinum toxin prevents release.

lessons.title: Adrenergic Transmission

levels.kid:
The fight-or-flight side of your autopilot uses a chemical note called **norepinephrine**. Your adrenal glands, which sit on top of your kidneys, also squirt out a cousin called **epinephrine**, or adrenaline.

Your body builds these notes from a building block in food called **tyrosine**, step by step, like building with blocks.

After the message is sent, the nerve sucks most of the notes back up to use again, like a vacuum cleaner. Some medicines block the vacuum, so the notes stay around longer and the message gets stronger.
levels.hs:
**Norepinephrine (NE)** is the transmitter of most sympathetic postganglionic neurons. **Epinephrine** is a hormone released mainly by the adrenal medulla. Together with dopamine they are called **catecholamines**.

**Synthesis**, step by step:
- Tyrosine → **DOPA** by tyrosine hydroxylase (the rate-limiting step)
- DOPA → **dopamine** by DOPA decarboxylase
- Dopamine is pumped into vesicles, where dopamine β-hydroxylase makes **norepinephrine**
- In the adrenal medulla, PNMT converts NE into **epinephrine**

**Release** happens when calcium enters the nerve ending. NE acts on **α and β adrenergic receptors**. It also acts on **α2 receptors** on its own nerve ending, which act as brakes and reduce further release.

**Termination**: most NE is taken back into the nerve by the **norepinephrine transporter (NET)**. Cocaine and tricyclic antidepressants block NET. Leftover NE is broken down by two enzymes, **MAO** and **COMT**. A breakdown product, **VMA**, and the metanephrines can be measured to detect adrenal tumors that make too many catecholamines (pheochromocytoma).

Some drugs work indirectly by pushing NE out of the nerve ending. That is why patients on **MAO inhibitors** must avoid foods rich in **tyramine**, like aged cheese: tyramine releases large amounts of NE and can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure.
levels.college:
**Biosynthesis.** **Tyrosine hydroxylase** (TH) hydroxylates tyrosine to L-DOPA using tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), O2 and Fe2+; it is rate-limiting and feedback-inhibited by catecholamines, and acutely activated by phosphorylation. **Metyrosine** inhibits TH (used in pheochromocytoma). **Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase** (AADC, pyridoxal phosphate-dependent) forms dopamine; carbidopa inhibits it peripherally. Dopamine enters vesicles via **VMAT2**, then **dopamine β-hydroxylase** (copper, ascorbate) forms NE inside the vesicle. In adrenal chromaffin cells, **PNMT** N-methylates NE to epinephrine; PNMT is induced by high local cortisol delivered through the intra-adrenal portal circulation.

**Storage and release.** VMAT2 is blocked irreversibly by **reserpine** (depleting stores) and reversibly by **tetrabenazine**. Ca2+-dependent exocytosis releases NE with ATP and neuropeptide Y.

**Presynaptic regulation.** α2A autoreceptors (Gi) inhibit release; presynaptic β2 receptors may facilitate it; heteroreceptors (M2, adenosine A1, opioid) inhibit.

**Termination.**
- **Uptake 1 (NET, SLC6A2)**: high-affinity neuronal reuptake removing most released NE. Blocked by cocaine, tricyclics and SNRIs.
- **Uptake 2**: extraneuronal, low-affinity (OCT3), important for circulating catecholamines.
- **MAO** (outer mitochondrial membrane; MAO-A prefers NE and serotonin, MAO-B prefers dopamine) and **COMT** (extraneuronal). End products: VMA and MHPG from NE/epinephrine, HVA from dopamine. **Plasma free metanephrines** (COMT products made within tumor cells) are the most sensitive screen for pheochromocytoma.

**Indirect sympathomimetics** (tyramine, ephedrine in part) enter via NET, displace NE from vesicles and reverse NET. Tyramine is normally destroyed by intestinal and hepatic MAO-A; under MAO inhibition it reaches nerve terminals and causes hypertensive crisis. **Guanethidine** accumulates in vesicles and blocks release. Indirect agents show **tachyphylaxis** as releasable stores deplete.
levels.phd:
Catecholamine signaling is tuned at every step by regulatory biochemistry. Tyrosine hydroxylase is controlled on several time scales: phosphorylation at Ser40 by PKA relieves catecholamine feedback inhibition within seconds; longer stress induces TH transcription (trans-synaptic induction) over hours to days. BH4 availability, set by GTP cyclohydrolase I, links catecholamine synthesis to inherited disorders: GCH1 mutations cause dopa-responsive dystonia, and AADC deficiency, now treated with AAV gene therapy into the putamen, is a severe infantile disorder.

**NET** is a Na+/Cl−-coupled symporter of the SLC6 family. Its reversal by amphetamine-class releasers depends on VMAT2 interaction, cytosolic accumulation, and transporter phosphorylation; this is mechanistically distinct from reuptake blockade, which only prolongs the life of exocytotically released NE. Interestingly, NET clears dopamine efficiently in the prefrontal cortex, where the dopamine transporter is sparse, which partly explains how NET inhibitors affect prefrontal dopamine.

**Metabolic topology** matters clinically. Sympathetic neurons contain MAO but little COMT, so intraneuronal deamination of leaked NE produces DHPG, the dominant metabolite in plasma. Metanephrines arise mostly within adrenal chromaffin cells and pheochromocytomas, which express membrane-bound COMT; that is why plasma free metanephrines remain elevated even when tumors secrete catecholamines episodically.

The **denervation supersensitivity** principle has two mechanisms: loss of reuptake (presynaptic, immediate after neuron loss, affecting NE but not drugs that are not NET substrates) and receptor upregulation (postsynaptic, developing over days to weeks). This distinction underlies pharmacologic pupil testing and the exaggerated pressor responses in autonomic failure, in which small doses of directly acting agonists produce large blood pressure rises.

The **tyramine pressor test** historically quantified MAO inhibition. Selective, reversible MAO-A inhibitors such as moclobemide and transdermal selegiline at lower exposure reduce, but do not abolish, dietary interactions.
levels.expert:
Practical adrenergic transmission is about predicting drug and food interactions and recognizing catecholamine excess.

**MAO inhibitor interactions.** Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats, fermented soy, tap beer) and indirect sympathomimetics such as pseudoephedrine can cause hypertensive crisis. Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, linezolid, which is itself a weak MAO inhibitor, meperidine, tramadol, methylene blue) risk serotonin syndrome. Methylene blue, used intraoperatively and for vasoplegia, is a potent MAO-A inhibitor; several serotonin syndrome cases followed its use in patients on SSRIs.

**Reuptake blockade in surgery.** Patients on tricyclics or SNRIs respond more strongly to directly acting catecholamines, while response to indirect agents like ephedrine may be blunted. Topical cocaine, used for its vasoconstriction in nasal and skull base surgery, combines local anesthesia with NET blockade; combined with epinephrine infiltration it can precipitate hypertension and arrhythmia.

**Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma.** Classic triad: episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with hypertension. Screen with plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines; false positives come from tricyclics, levodopa and stress. Preoperative preparation is **α-blockade first** (phenoxybenzamine or a selective α1 blocker), then β-blockade only after α-blockade, because unopposed α stimulation after β-blockade removes β2 vasodilation and can precipitate hypertensive crisis. Volume expansion follows α-blockade. Metyrosine can be added to reduce synthesis.

**Neurocritical care.** After subarachnoid hemorrhage or severe brain injury, catecholamine surges cause neurogenic stunned myocardium and Takotsubo-like dysfunction, ECG changes and neurogenic pulmonary edema. Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity after traumatic brain injury produces bursts of tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia and posturing; nonselective β-blockers, α2 agonists, gabapentin and opioids are used to blunt episodes.

VMAT2 loads vesicles; reserpine blocks it irreversibly

Tumor cells contain COMT and continuously metabolize leaking catecholamines

It is a potent MAO-A inhibitor that can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs

Increased NE synthesis by the remaining sympathetic nerve terminals

A stronger baroreflex that overshoots and amplifies pressor responses

lessons.title: Receptor Subtypes and Organ Responses

levels.kid:
Each chemical note needs the right **catcher** on a cell. Different catchers make different things happen, even with the same note.

Think of a light switch and a doorbell. Pressing one turns on a light; pressing the other rings a bell. Your body has catchers with names like **alpha**, **beta** and **muscarinic**.

Beta catchers on the heart make it beat faster. Beta catchers in the lungs open the airways, which is why some asthma inhalers work on them. Alpha catchers squeeze blood vessels. Muscarinic catchers slow the heart and make spit and tears.

If you know the catchers, you can guess what a medicine will do!
levels.hs:
Autonomic drugs make sense once you know which receptor sits on which organ.

**Adrenergic receptors** (respond to NE and epinephrine):
- **α1**: contracts smooth muscle in blood vessels (raises blood pressure), dilates the pupil, tightens the bladder neck.
- **α2**: on nerve endings, reduces NE release; in the brain, lowers sympathetic outflow.
- **β1**: heart: faster rate, stronger contraction; kidney: renin release.
- **β2**: relaxes smooth muscle in airways (bronchodilation) and in blood vessels of skeletal muscle; raises blood sugar; causes tremor.
- **β3**: breaks down fat and relaxes the bladder wall.

**Muscarinic receptors** (respond to ACh):
- **M2**: heart: slower rate.
- **M3**: contracts airway, gut and bladder muscle, constricts the pupil, increases secretions (saliva, sweat, tears, mucus).

**Examples:** albuterol, a β2 agonist, opens the airways in asthma. Metoprolol, a β1 blocker, slows the heart. Phenylephrine, an α1 agonist, raises blood pressure. Atropine, a muscarinic blocker, speeds the heart and dries secretions.

The eye shows both systems: muscarinic receptors on the circular sphincter constrict the pupil, and α1 receptors on the radial dilator muscle widen it.
levels.college:
**Adrenoceptors** are GPCRs with characteristic coupling:
- **α1 (Gq)**: vascular smooth muscle contraction, pupillary dilator (mydriasis), prostate and bladder neck contraction, pilomotor muscles, hepatic glycogenolysis.
- **α2 (Gi)**: presynaptic inhibition of NE release; central reduction of sympathetic outflow (clonidine, dexmedetomidine); inhibition of insulin secretion and lipolysis; platelet aggregation; decreased aqueous humor production.
- **β1 (Gs)**: positive chronotropy, inotropy, dromotropy and lusitropy; renin release from juxtaglomerular cells.
- **β2 (Gs)**: relaxation of bronchial, vascular (skeletal muscle beds), uterine and detrusor smooth muscle; hepatic glycogenolysis; K+ shift into cells via Na+/K+-ATPase; skeletal muscle tremor.
- **β3 (Gs)**: lipolysis, detrusor relaxation (mirabegron, vibegron).

**Muscarinic receptors**:
- **M1 (Gq)**: CNS, enteric and autonomic ganglia (slow EPSP).
- **M2 (Gi)**: SA node and AV node slowing (via GIRK/IKACh), presynaptic inhibition.
- **M3 (Gq)**: bronchoconstriction and bronchial secretion, GI motility and secretion, detrusor contraction, pupillary sphincter (miosis) and ciliary muscle (accommodation for near vision), salivary and sweat glands, endothelial NO release causing vasodilation.

**Dopamine D1 (Gs)**: renal and mesenteric vasodilation.

**Eye pharmacology:**
- Pupil: M3 sphincter (miosis) vs α1 dilator (mydriasis).
- Aqueous humor: β-blockers (timolol) and α2 agonists reduce production; prostaglandin analogs increase uveoscleral outflow; muscarinic agonists contract the ciliary muscle and open the trabecular meshwork.

**Most blood vessels have no parasympathetic innervation**, yet injected ACh vasodilates them through endothelial M3 receptors and NO. **Epinephrine** shows dose-dependence: at low concentrations β effects predominate (β2 vasodilation, possibly lowering diastolic pressure), at higher ones α1 vasoconstriction dominates.
levels.phd:
Receptor pharmacology in vivo integrates coupling, receptor reserve, compartmentalization and reflexes.

**Signaling diversity.** β2 receptors can switch from Gs to Gi after PKA phosphorylation, and β-arrestin recruitment drives desensitization, internalization and separate signaling. Biased agonism (for example, β-arrestin–biased β-blockers such as carvedilol in cell assays) is an active research area, though its clinical relevance is uncertain. Cardiac β1 and β2 receptors are compartmentalized: β1 cAMP signals spread broadly, whereas β2 signals are confined near T-tubules, and in heart failure this compartmentation breaks down.

**Receptor reserve** determines selectivity in practice. A partial agonist can act as a full agonist in tissues with high receptor density and as an antagonist in tissues with low density. "Selectivity" of β1-blockers (metoprolol, bisoprolol) is relative: at higher concentrations they block β2 and can precipitate bronchospasm in susceptible asthmatics.

**Subtype complexity.** Nine adrenoceptor subtypes exist (α1A/B/D, α2A/B/C, β1–3). α1A dominates in prostate, so tamsulosin (α1A-preferring) relieves urinary obstruction with less orthostasis; α1A blockade in the iris dilator causes **intraoperative floppy iris syndrome** during cataract surgery. α2A mediates sedation and antihypertensive action; α2B mediates the transient hypertension seen with rapid intravenous α2 agonist loading, through vascular smooth muscle.

**Epinephrine reversal** is a classic integrative experiment: after α-blockade, epinephrine lowers blood pressure because unopposed β2 vasodilation is unmasked. Norepinephrine, with weak β2 activity, simply loses its pressor effect.

**Potassium.** β2-mediated Na+/K+-ATPase activation explains hypokalemia after albuterol or stress catecholamines, and the use of inhaled β2 agonists to shift potassium into cells in hyperkalemia. Nonselective β-blockers impair potassium disposal after exercise.

**Metabolism.** β2 and α1 hepatic effects plus α2 suppression of insulin create stress hyperglycemia; β-blockers mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (tremor, palpitations) but not sweating, which is cholinergic.
levels.expert:
Receptor maps become bedside predictions. Before giving any autonomic drug, a clinician runs through the organs and asks what the drug's receptor profile will do, and what the reflexes will do in response.

**Vasopressor choice in neurocritical care** follows the map:
- **Phenylephrine** (pure α1): raises systemic vascular resistance, often with reflex bradycardia; useful when tachycardia is unwanted, but it can lower cardiac output.
- **Norepinephrine** (α1 > β1): raises pressure with preserved or improved output; first-line for most shock states and common for cerebral perfusion pressure targets.
- **Epinephrine** (β1, β2, α1): strong inotropy and chronotropy, raises lactate and glucose through β2 effects.
- **Dobutamine** (mainly β1, some β2): inotropy with possible hypotension from vasodilation.
- **Dopamine** has dose-dependent receptor recruitment but more arrhythmias than norepinephrine in shock trials, so it has fallen out of favor.

**Dexmedetomidine**, an α2A agonist, gives sedation with preserved respiratory drive and cooperative arousability, useful for awake craniotomy and neuro checks. Expect bradycardia and hypotension; rapid loading may transiently raise blood pressure through α2B.

**Predictable traps:**
- β-blocker drops (timolol) are absorbed systemically through the nasolacrimal duct and can cause bradycardia or bronchospasm.
- Mydriatics before a neuro exam: always document dilating drops, because a pharmacologically dilated pupil mimics a third nerve palsy. A pupil dilated by an antimuscarinic will not constrict to pilocarpine, unlike a pupil from oculomotor nerve compression, which still constricts.
- Tamsulosin history matters before cataract surgery (floppy iris).
- Nonselective β-blockers in asthma or with epinephrine treatment for anaphylaxis can cause refractory reactions; glucagon bypasses the β receptor via its own Gs-coupled receptor.

**Sweating is sympathetic but cholinergic**, so anticholinergic toxicity gives hot, dry skin, while sympathomimetic toxicity gives diaphoresis. That single fact distinguishes two toxidromes at a glance.

keyPoints: α1 Gq: vasoconstriction, mydriasis; α2 Gi: ↓NE release, central sympatholysis
β1 Gs: ↑HR, contractility, renin; β2 Gs: bronchodilation, vasodilation, K+ into cells, tremor; β3: lipolysis, detrusor relaxation
M2 Gi: slows heart; M3 Gq: smooth muscle contraction, secretions, miosis, accommodation, endothelial NO
Pupil: M3 sphincter (miosis) vs α1 dilator (mydriasis)
Epinephrine reversal: after α-blockade, epinephrine lowers BP via β2
Sweat glands are sympathetic but cholinergic (muscarinic)

test.explain: β2 relaxes airway smooth muscle; that's how albuterol works.

test.explain: β1 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells stimulate renin release.

test.explain: M3 on the circular sphincter muscle constricts the pupil.

test.explain: α1 → Gq → PLC → IP3/DAG → Ca2+ → smooth muscle contraction.

Opening GIRK K+ channels and lowering cAMP
test.explain: M2 via Gi lowers cAMP and Gβγ opens GIRK (IKACh), hyperpolarizing nodal cells.

choices: It acts on α1 receptors and relaxes the arterial muscle
It blocks NE release from sympathetic nerve endings
It stimulates endothelial M3 receptors to release NO
It is converted to epinephrine, which dilates via β2
test.explain: Endothelial M3 → NO → smooth muscle relaxation (Furchgott's discovery).

test.q: β3 agonists such as mirabegron are used for:
test.explain: β3 relaxes the detrusor muscle.

test.q: A patient pretreated with an α-blocker is given epinephrine. Blood pressure will most likely:
test.explain: Epinephrine reversal: β2 vasodilation is unmasked.

test.q: Which receptor subtype do clonidine and dexmedetomidine stimulate?
test.explain: Central α2 activation reduces sympathetic outflow and causes sedation.

test.q: β2 stimulation shifts ___ into cells, which can lower its blood level.
test.explain: Via Na+/K+-ATPase; inhaled albuterol is used in hyperkalemia.

test.q: Name the receptor on the radial (dilator) muscle of the iris.
test.explain: α1 contracts the dilator, causing mydriasis.

test.q: Sympathetic fibers to sweat glands release ___.
test.explain: Sweat glands are sympathetic cholinergic, acting on muscarinic receptors.

Beta catchers on the heart make it:
Some asthma inhalers work on beta catchers in the:

advancedTest.q: A comatose patient has one dilated pupil. Pilocarpine drops fail to constrict it. Most likely cause?
advancedTest.explain: Antimuscarinic blockade prevents constriction to pilocarpine; a CN III compression pupil still constricts.

choices: Direct β1 stimulation of the heart
α2B receptors on vascular smooth muscle

advancedTest.explain: Glucagon acts through its own Gs-coupled receptor, increasing cardiac cAMP.

lessons.title: Autonomic Reflexes and Dual Innervation

levels.kid:
Your body has sensors in big blood vessels in your neck and chest. They check your blood pressure all the time, like a thermostat checks the temperature in a house.

If your blood pressure goes up too high, the sensors tell your brain, and your brain slows your heart down. If the pressure drops, like when you stand up fast, your brain speeds your heart up and squeezes your blood vessels.

Most organs get messages from both autopilot sides, a gas pedal and a brake. That way your body can go faster or slower whenever it needs to.
levels.hs:
**Dual innervation** means most organs receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, usually with opposite effects. The heart, gut, bladder, eyes and airways are examples. Some tissues get only sympathetic nerves: most blood vessels, sweat glands and the adrenal medulla.

At rest, one side usually dominates in each organ, called its **predominant tone**. The heart, gut and bladder are mostly under parasympathetic tone. Blood vessels are under sympathetic tone.

The **baroreceptor reflex** keeps blood pressure stable from moment to moment. Stretch sensors in the **carotid sinus** and **aortic arch** detect pressure and send signals to the brainstem.
- When pressure rises, the brainstem increases vagal (parasympathetic) activity and reduces sympathetic activity: the heart slows.
- When pressure falls, the opposite happens: the heart speeds up and vessels constrict.

This reflex explains why drugs can have "backwards" effects. **Phenylephrine** constricts vessels and raises blood pressure, so the heart rate actually falls (reflex bradycardia). **Vasodilators** like hydralazine lower blood pressure, so the heart speeds up (reflex tachycardia).

When you stand up quickly, blood pools in your legs. The baroreflex normally fixes this in seconds; if it fails, you get dizzy (**orthostatic hypotension**).
levels.college:
**Baroreflex arc.** Carotid sinus baroreceptors signal via the glossopharyngeal nerve (Hering's nerve); aortic arch receptors via the vagus. Afferents terminate in the **nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)**. Increased firing excites vagal preganglionic neurons (nucleus ambiguus, dorsal motor nucleus) and, via the caudal ventrolateral medulla, inhibits the **rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM)**, the main source of sympathetic vasomotor drive.

**Drug responses through the reflex:**
- **Phenylephrine** (α1): ↑SVR, ↑BP, reflex ↓HR.
- **Norepinephrine** (α1 + β1): ↑BP; reflex vagal slowing can offset direct β1 chronotropy, so HR is unchanged or falls.
- **Epinephrine** at low infusion rates: β1 ↑HR, β2 ↓diastolic pressure, wider pulse pressure.
- **Isoproterenol** (β1 + β2): ↓diastolic and mean pressure; direct plus reflex tachycardia.
- Vasodilators (hydralazine, nitroprusside, dihydropyridines): reflex tachycardia and renin release, which is why hydralazine is paired with a β-blocker.
- **Atropine** abolishes vagally mediated reflex bradycardia.

**Ganglionic blockade reveals predominant tone.** Blocking NN receptors removes whichever division dominates each organ:
- Heart (parasympathetic dominant): tachycardia.
- Arterioles and veins (sympathetic): vasodilation, orthostatic hypotension.
- Iris (parasympathetic): mydriasis; ciliary muscle: cycloplegia.
- GI tract (parasympathetic): reduced motility, constipation.
- Bladder (parasympathetic): urinary retention.
- Salivary glands (parasympathetic): dry mouth.
- Sweat glands (sympathetic cholinergic): anhidrosis.

**Other reflexes:** the Valsalva maneuver tests baroreflex integrity; vasovagal syncope is a sudden vagal surge with sympathetic withdrawal; the Bainbridge reflex raises HR with atrial stretch.

**Denervated transplanted heart:** no vagal tone, so resting HR is higher; atropine has no chronotropic effect; responses to exercise rely on circulating catecholamines.
levels.phd:
The baroreflex is a negative-feedback controller with a sigmoid stimulus–response curve centered near the prevailing mean arterial pressure. Its **gain** (heart rate change per mmHg) is measurable by the modified Oxford method (sequential nitroprusside and phenylephrine boluses) or spontaneous sequence analysis. The reflex **resets**: in chronic hypertension and during exercise (via central command and muscle afferents), the curve shifts rightward, which is why it buffers short-term fluctuations but does not set long-term pressure; renal pressure natriuresis does. Still, baroreflex activation therapy (carotid sinus stimulation) lowers pressure chronically in some patients, showing that central integration contributes to long-term set points.

The cardiac vagal and sympathetic limbs differ in kinetics. Vagal effects on the SA node act within a single beat via ACh, GIRK channels and rapid hydrolysis by AChE; sympathetic effects take seconds via cAMP signaling and slow NE clearance. This explains why high-frequency **heart rate variability** (respiratory sinus arrhythmia) indexes vagal modulation, and why atropine abolishes it.

Interactions between the limbs are nonlinear (**accentuated antagonism**): vagal slowing is stronger when sympathetic tone is high, partly through presynaptic M2 inhibition of NE release and postsynaptic Gi opposition of cAMP. Conversely, neuropeptide Y released during intense sympathetic activity inhibits ACh release, blunting vagal control for minutes.

**Cushing reflex.** Rising intracranial pressure compromises brainstem perfusion; the medulla responds with intense sympathetic discharge to raise systemic pressure and restore cerebral perfusion pressure. Hypertension then activates baroreceptors, producing bradycardia. With brainstem distortion, respiration becomes irregular. The **Cushing triad** is a late sign of impending herniation.

Autonomic dysreflexia illustrates spinal reflexes without supraspinal modulation: afferent input below a high cord lesion triggers segmental sympathetic discharge with splanchnic vasoconstriction, while baroreflex-driven vagal bradycardia and vasodilation above the lesion cannot correct it because descending inhibitory pathways are cut.
levels.expert:
For a clinician, reflexes explain most "paradoxical" vital signs.

**Read the pair, not the number.** Hypertension with bradycardia in a patient with a brain injury is the **Cushing response** until proven otherwise: check pupils, level of consciousness and get imaging. Lowering blood pressure in that patient may drop cerebral perfusion pressure, so the priority is treating raised intracranial pressure (head elevation, osmotherapy, CSF drainage, surgical decompression), not antihypertensives alone.

**Vasopressor choice and reflexes.** Phenylephrine in a patient who is already bradycardic can drive heart rate lower; norepinephrine or ephedrine is often better. Conversely, phenylephrine is useful when tachycardia is harmful, as in aortic stenosis. In the operating room, traction on the eye or carotid sinus, or on the dura and trigeminal territory (the **trigeminocardiac reflex**, seen in skull base, cerebellopontine angle and transsphenoidal surgery), can cause sudden bradycardia or asystole. The first response is to stop the stimulus; atropine or glycopyrrolate is used if bradycardia persists.

**Carotid surgery and stenting** manipulate the carotid sinus: bradycardia and hypotension during stent balloon inflation are common, and postoperative baroreflex dysfunction causes labile blood pressure, sometimes hyperperfusion syndrome.

**Autonomic dysreflexia** in a patient with a lesion above T6: severe hypertension, pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the lesion, often with bradycardia. Sit the patient upright, loosen tight clothing, check the bladder catheter and bowel, and use a fast-acting antihypertensive if pressure stays high. Untreated, it can cause stroke or seizures.

**Orthostatic hypotension** workup: stop offending drugs first (α1-blockers, nitrates, diuretics, tricyclics, levodopa). Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, diabetic autonomic neuropathy) shows little heart rate rise despite a big pressure drop, which separates it from volume depletion. Treatments include midodrine (α1 agonist prodrug), droxidopa (NE precursor) and fludrocortisone, with care about supine hypertension.

keyPoints: Dual innervation: most organs get both divisions; vessels, sweat glands and adrenal medulla get only sympathetic
Baroreflex: carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) → NTS → ↑vagal, ↓RVLM sympathetic output
Phenylephrine → reflex bradycardia; vasodilators → reflex tachycardia
Ganglionic blockade removes predominant tone: tachycardia, hypotension, mydriasis, dry mouth, retention, constipation
Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) signals raised ICP
Transplanted heart: no vagal tone; atropine has no chronotropic effect

test.explain: α1-mediated hypertension triggers baroreflex vagal slowing.

test.q: Carotid sinus baroreceptors send afferent signals via:
test.explain: Hering's nerve is a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve; aortic arch afferents travel in CN X.

test.q: Baroreceptor afferents first synapse in the:

test.q: Why is hydralazine often combined with a β-blocker?

test.q: Which tissue receives sympathetic but not parasympathetic innervation?

test.q: In a heart transplant recipient, atropine will:

test.explain: It indicates brainstem compromise and impending herniation.

test.q: The main source of sympathetic vasomotor drive in the brainstem is the rostral ___ medulla.
test.explain: The RVLM is inhibited by the baroreflex via the caudal ventrolateral medulla.

test.q: What is the term for a drop in blood pressure on standing?
test.explain: It reflects failure of the baroreflex or low volume.

test.q: Atrial stretch raising heart rate is the ___ reflex.
test.explain: The Bainbridge reflex opposes the baroreflex during volume loading.

kidTest.q: Blood pressure sensors are found in:
choices: Big blood vessels in the neck and chest
The tips of your toes and feet
The hair on top of your head
kidTest.explain: They sit in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.

kidTest.q: If blood pressure goes too high, the brain:
kidTest.explain: The reflex brings pressure back down.

kidTest.q: When you stand up fast, your heart:
kidTest.explain: It speeds up to keep blood going to your brain.

kidTest.q: Most organs get messages from:
choices: Both autopilot sides, a gas pedal and a brake
The radio playing inside your head
The organ's own clock, without nerve signals
kidTest.explain: Dual innervation lets the body speed up or slow down.

kidTest.q: The blood pressure sensors work like a house's ___ (it checks temperature).

advancedTest.q: During transsphenoidal or cerebellopontine angle surgery, sudden bradycardia with manipulation is most likely the:
advancedTest.explain: Trigeminal stimulation triggers vagal bradycardia or asystole; stop the stimulus first.

advancedTest.q: 'Accentuated antagonism' refers to:
choices: Vagal slowing being stronger when sympathetic tone is high
Sympathetic effects being stronger when vagal tone is high
advancedTest.explain: Presynaptic M2 inhibition of NE release and Gi opposition of cAMP magnify vagal effects under high sympathetic drive.

advancedTest.q: A patient with orthostatic BP drop of 30 mmHg systolic and a heart rate rise of only 5 bpm most likely has:
choices: Anxiety or a panic response on standing
advancedTest.explain: A blunted heart rate response despite a large pressure fall points to baroreflex/autonomic failure.

advancedTest.q: In a patient with autonomic dysreflexia, the first step is:
choices: Lay the patient flat and give an IV fluid bolus right away
Give an inhaled β-agonist to bring the blood pressure down
Sit upright and find the trigger (bladder, bowel, tight clothing)
Give IV atropine first to treat the slow heart rate
advancedTest.explain: Upright posture lowers pressure; removing the noxious stimulus is the definitive fix.
